claims.text: The overall tribocorrosion degradation of HEAs is governed by the formation and stability of an in-situ, wear-induced passive oxide or composite layer.
A dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide can protect AlCrTiZrMo HEA films.
Thermal treatment in air can promote formation of a dense protective oxide on an AlCrTiZrMo HEA film.
B addition can promote formation of a dense, adherent passive oxide film on an HEA surface.
A stable surface oxide limits corrosion damage.
A stable surface oxide retards wear-induced degradation.
The proposed as-deposited or as-cast starting HEA has a reactive amorphous or nanocrystalline surface without a well-developed protective oxide.
The induced oxide or composite film is continuous and adherent and resists mechanical spallation.
The induced oxide or composite film acts as a barrier to corrosive agents.
Sliding wear removes surface material and continuously exposes fresh metal.
Freshly exposed metal rapidly forms a passive oxide during tribocorrosion.
Competition between mechanical film removal and repassivation determines net degradation.
A pretreated HEA will have lower total tribocorrosion mass loss than the untreated baseline.
The predicted reduction in total degradation will arise primarily from a reduced corrosion component.
The wear contribution may remain similar after pretreatment.
Pretreatment will produce lower corrosion current density and potential shifts indicating improved passivation.
The protective effect should hold at moderate to high contact pressures because those pressures permit sufficient passive-film regeneration.
The protective effect may fail under extreme loads or abrasive conditions because mechanical removal becomes excessive.
The protective effect may fail in alloys lacking the necessary oxide-forming elements.

Failure of the thermally treated group to show statistically significant reductions in both the corrosion component and overall mass loss would falsify the proposed passive-oxide governance mechanism.
